prompt_free_text:
This paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: moving spoken dialogue agents beyond turn-based, half-duplex interaction toward genuinely synchronous, full-duplex behavior with overlaps, backchannels, and latency-aware turn-taking. The central idea is to adapt a pretrained autoregressive LLM into a wall-clock-synchronous dialogue model by interleaving two speaker streams with periodic synchronization tokens, training on deduplicated speech-unit sequences, and explicitly predicting short future chunks to tolerate input latency. The paper is ambitious, timely, and generally well motivated. It also presents a fairly compelling empirical story: large gains in semantic meaningfulness over dGSLM, competitive or slightly improved turn-taking naturalness, and a plausible recipe for leveraging abundant text dialogue data plus synthetic speech to compensate for the scarcity of real duplex speech corpora.

At a high level, I found the paper interesting and potentially impactful. The framing is strong: most current “voice assistants” are indeed still fundamentally turn-based, and the paper correctly identifies synchrony and latency as core obstacles rather than superficial engineering details. The proposed formulation is also elegant in spirit. Instead of building a bespoke duplex architecture from scratch, the authors retrofit a standard decoder-only LLM with a temporal tokenization scheme that lets it operate on synchronized chunks. This is conceptually appealing because it preserves compatibility with text-pretrained LLMs and their semantic strengths. The empirical results, especially the large human-rated meaningfulness gains over dGSLM, suggest that this design choice is fruitful.

The strongest contribution, in my view, is the combination of three ideas: periodic synchronization tokens to anchor time, deduplicated speech-unit modeling to preserve semantic density, and one-step-ahead user-chunk prediction to handle real-world latency. Each of these is individually sensible, and together they form a coherent system-level proposal. The paper also does a good job motivating why full-duplex interaction is not just “interruptibility” but requires continuous readiness to both listen and speak. This distinction is important and often glossed over in prior work.

That said, while the paper is promising, I have several concerns about evaluation rigor, clarity of the claimed novelty, and the extent to which the experiments truly validate “full-duplex dialogue agents” rather than improved spoken dialogue continuation models.

First, the paper’s strongest empirical gains are on semantic meaningfulness, but these gains may derive substantially from leveraging Llama-3 text pretraining and large synthetic dialogue corpora rather than from the synchronous/full-duplex formulation itself. This is not a flaw in the method, but it complicates the attribution of improvements. The baseline dGSLM is a speech-only model with a different architecture and training regime, so the comparison conflates multiple factors: pretrained text knowledge, synthetic data scale, tokenization choices, and the synchronization mechanism. As a result, the paper convincingly shows that the overall system is better, but less convincingly isolates which parts are necessary for the gains. An ablation study would be essential here. For example: what happens without synchronization tokens, without deduplication, without stage 2, without future user-chunk prediction, or with a simpler turn-based LLM baseline trained on the same synthetic and real data? Without such controls, it is difficult to assess how much of the improvement is due specifically to the proposed synchronous modeling.

Second, the evaluation of semantics via ASR transcription followed by perplexity under a text dialogue model is only an indirect proxy. It may be reasonable as one signal, but it is vulnerable to ASR errors, especially under overlap, and the paper explicitly says overlapping speech is ignored when converting to turn-based text. This is problematic because overlap is one of the central phenomena the paper claims to model. If the semantic metric discards overlap, then it may systematically miss failures or successes unique to full-duplex interaction. Moreover, perplexity under an external text dialogue model is not obviously aligned with dialogue quality or coherence in spoken settings. The human meaningfulness MOS helps address this, and those results are much more convincing, but the automatic semantic evaluation should be interpreted more cautiously than the paper currently does.

Third, the naturalness evaluation based on correlations of average IPU, pause, and FTO durations is useful but limited. Correlation of aggregate durations does not necessarily imply locally appropriate turn-taking behavior. A model could match global statistics while still producing unnatural interruptions or mistimed backchannels in context. Since the paper’s central claim is about synchronous interaction, I would have liked more event-level analyses: precision/recall for backchannels, overlap rate distributions, gap distributions conditioned on turn endings, interruption recovery behavior, or human judgments specifically targeted at overlap appropriateness and responsiveness. The current MOS naturalness scores are nearly flat across systems and close to re-synthesized ground truth, which is encouraging but also suggests the metric may not be sensitive enough to the claimed advances.

Fourth, the “interaction” setting is still simulated as model-model interaction, not human-model interaction. I understand why this is done, but it weakens the claim that the system functions as a practical full-duplex dialogue agent. In particular, the user-side model is itself generated from the same modeling assumptions and tokenization pipeline, which may make the interaction easier than real deployment with human speech variability, ASR/noise issues, hesitations, disfluencies, and unpredictable timing. The paper does acknowledge latency and proposes a mechanism for one-chunk delayed input, but there is no end-to-end real-time experiment with actual users or even replayed human speech under controlled network delays. As a result, the paper demonstrates a plausible simulation of latency-tolerant duplex interaction, but not yet a convincing real-world full-duplex agent.

Fifth, the interpolation heuristic used to reconstruct periodic HuBERT tokens from deduplicated chunks seems under-justified. The paper states that repeated tokens are restored by equal repetition within a chunk and that the resulting timing error is perceptually negligible, even at 240 ms chunk size. This may be true, but the evidence presented is anecdotal. Since this interpolation is central to speech synthesis quality and timing fidelity, it deserves quantitative analysis. For example, how much does interpolation distort duration distributions relative to original token sequences? Does it affect overlap timing or pause realism? The resynthesized-ground-truth topline partially reflects tokenization/reconstruction loss, but it does not isolate the interpolation heuristic itself.

Sixth, the training recipe is interesting but underspecified in several places. The paper mentions 212k hours of synthetic spoken dialogue and 2k hours of real dialogue, but it is not sufficiently clear which text datasets are used, how they are filtered, how many dialogues versus turns they contain, whether train/test contamination with Fisher/CANDOR topics is possible, and how the synthetic speech diversity is controlled given only 10 Bark speaker presets. Since the paper’s main practical claim is that synthetic spoken dialogue can bootstrap full-duplex modeling, more transparency about data composition is important. Similarly, the stage-1 mixed text/speech training strategy is intriguing, but the exact truncated normal schedule, optimization details, and stability issues are not described in enough detail for reproducibility.

Seventh, the novelty relative to prior multimodal/speech LLM work is meaningful but perhaps somewhat overstated. The paper’s main novelty is not simply “adding time to LLMs,” but a specific chunk-synchronous interleaving scheme plus latency-aware future prediction for duplex dialogue. That is a worthwhile contribution. However, the paper should more carefully distinguish what is fundamentally new from what is an adaptation of existing speech-unit language modeling and interleaving ideas. In particular, interleaving modalities or streams, deduplicating speech units, and using special tokens for structure all have precedents. The novelty lies in the synchronization protocol and deployment framing, and the paper would benefit from sharpening that point.

There are also some methodological and presentation issues. The paper repeatedly uses “full-duplex” in a broad conversational sense, but in communications terminology full-duplex usually means simultaneous bidirectional transmission capability, not necessarily human-like overlap management. The authors do define their intended meaning, but some readers may still find the terminology slightly overloaded. The paper also has a number of writing issues and typos that should be cleaned up: grammatical errors, repeated words, and some awkward phrasing in the training and evaluation sections. Figure 7 is missing in the provided content, which makes it impossible to inspect one of the key interaction results. Some tables are also a bit hard to interpret without clearer significance testing. For example, the MOS differences between SyncLLM-F and SyncLLM-F-F/SyncLLM-F-C are modest; it would help to know which differences are statistically significant.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has substantial merit. The human evaluation results are particularly notable. A roughly +2.2 gain in meaningfulness MOS over dGSLM is large, and the fact that naturalness remains comparable suggests the model is not simply trading timing quality for semantic quality. The out-of-distribution results on CANDOR are also encouraging, especially given training on Fisher only. More broadly, the paper advances an important perspective: spoken dialogue agents should be modeled as temporally grounded, continuously interactive systems rather than text chat models with speech I/O wrappers. That conceptual shift is valuable.

To strengthen the paper, I would strongly recommend the following additions or clarifications. Most importantly, include ablations that isolate the contribution of synchronization tokens, deduplication, future user-chunk prediction, and each training stage. A same-backbone baseline trained without synchronous interleaving would be especially informative. Second, add more targeted full-duplex metrics: overlap frequency, backchannel appropriateness, response onset latency, interruption handling, and perhaps human preference tests specifically about conversational flow rather than overall naturalness. Third, clarify the deployment pipeline: how exactly is real user speech tokenized online, what latency budget is assumed for unit extraction and vocoding, and how does the system behave under packet jitter or ASR/tokenization errors? Fourth, provide more detail on synthetic data generation and reproducibility. Fifth, if possible, include at least a small real-user study or replay-based evaluation with actual human speech and injected network delays.

My overall assessment is positive but not unreservedly so. The paper proposes a compelling direction and a technically coherent method, and it presents strong evidence that LLM-based synchronous spoken dialogue modeling can substantially improve semantic quality over prior speech-only duplex models. However, the current evaluation does not fully substantiate the strongest claims about real-world full-duplex interaction, and the lack of ablations makes it hard to disentangle where the gains come from. I would lean toward acceptance if the venue values ambitious systems papers and emerging directions, but I would expect a revision to tighten the empirical case and clarify the contribution boundaries.

In summary, this is a strong and interesting paper with clear potential impact. Its main strengths are the importance of the problem, the elegant synchronization formulation, the practical synthetic-data training recipe, and the substantial human-rated gains in meaningfulness. Its main weaknesses are insufficient ablation, reliance on indirect automatic metrics, limited validation of true interactive deployment, and some underdeveloped analysis of timing fidelity and overlap behavior. With stronger experimental isolation and more direct duplex evaluation, this could become a highly influential contribution.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes SyncLLM, a decoder-only LLM-based framework for full-duplex spoken dialogue. The core idea is to synchronize an autoregressive LLM with wall-clock time by inserting periodic speaker/synchronization tokens and modeling interleaved speech-unit chunks for both interlocutors. To mitigate redundancy in HuBERT token streams, the method predicts deduplicated unit sequences and reconstructs periodic streams via interpolation. The training recipe uses three stages: synthetic turn-based speech dialogue from text, synthetic full-duplex dialogue without overlaps, and final finetuning on ~2k hours of real dual-channel dialogue. Experiments compare against dGSLM using ASR-based semantic perplexity, turn-taking statistics, human MOS for meaningfulness/naturalness, and simulated interaction under one-chunk latency. Results suggest substantially improved semantic quality over dGSLM while maintaining comparable naturalness and some robustness to latency and domain shift.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: moving from turn-based spoken agents to genuinely synchronous/full-duplex interaction.
Conceptually elegant formulation that adapts a standard autoregressive LLM to wall-clock synchronized dialogue via periodic synchronization tokens rather than requiring a bespoke architecture.
Strong practical motivation and clear systems framing around latency tolerance, overlapping speech, backchannels, and streaming interaction.
Effective use of large-scale synthetic data to compensate for scarce real spoken dialogue data; the three-stage curriculum is plausible and practically valuable.
Empirical results show large gains over dGSLM on semantic meaningfulness, including human evaluation and ASR-based text perplexity.
Includes both in-distribution and OOD evaluation (Fisher/CANDOR), which strengthens claims of generalization.
Human evaluation is reasonably sized at the item level and reports confidence intervals/standard errors.
The paper is generally well written and the token formatting / synchronization mechanism is explained clearly.
weaknesses: The central claim of full-duplex capability is only partially validated: the interaction setting is simulated via LLM-LLM interaction rather than real human-agent online interaction with actual network, ASR, buffering, and user behavior.
The evaluation of semantics via ASR transcription and text perplexity is indirect and potentially confounded by ASR errors, overlap removal, and the choice of reference text model.

Naturalness evaluation relies on coarse correlation of aggregate turn-taking statistics rather than direct measures of overlap timing accuracy, interruption appropriateness, or backchannel usefulness.
The comparison baseline set is narrow; dGSLM is the main baseline, but stronger modern speech-text or cascaded streaming systems are not included.
The interpolation heuristic for reconstructing deduplicated tokens is acknowledged to be inaccurate, but its effect is not rigorously quantified beyond anecdotal perceptual claims.
Ablations are limited: it is unclear how much each component (deduplication, periodic sync tokens, future user-chunk prediction, synthetic stages) contributes to final performance.
The paper does not provide enough detail on training compute, optimization stability, inference latency budget, or deployment constraints for reproducibility and practical assessment.
Human MOS naturalness scores are roughly at parity or slightly lower than baseline in some settings, which weakens the claim of maintaining naturalness under full-duplex interaction.
methodological_flaws: The latency-tolerance claim is not fully empirically validated. Simulating one-chunk delayed interaction between two instances of the same modeling framework is not equivalent to demonstrating robustness in a real streaming deployment with actual user speech, packet jitter, ASR/VAD errors, and end-to-end system latency.

The semantic evaluation pipeline discards overlapping speech when converting generated dialogues to turn-based text, which removes precisely the phenomena the paper claims to model. This may bias evaluation toward turn-based coherence and under-evaluate whether overlapping/full-duplex behavior preserves meaning.

Using ASR-transcribed generations and perplexity under an external text dialogue model is an indirect metric whose validity depends on ASR quality and the calibration/domain of the text model. No sensitivity analysis is provided to show conclusions are robust to ASR/model choice.

The naturalness metric computes Pearson correlation of average event durations between generations and ground truth. Correlation of averages is a weak proxy for conversational naturalness and does not establish that generated timing distributions or event placements are realistic at the utterance level.

The interpolation procedure assumes equal repetition of deduplicated tokens within a chunk when reconstructing periodic HuBERT streams. This is a lossy heuristic that can distort duration/prosody, yet the paper provides no objective reconstruction error analysis or ablation against alternatives.

The claim that Stage 2 'models timing within an utterance' and Stage 3 learns turn-taking cues is plausible but not causally established; no controlled ablation isolates whether gains come from synthetic data scale, LLM initialization, token deduplication, or synchronization design.

The baseline comparison may not be fully fair because dGSLM is speech-only while SyncLLM leverages a large text-pretrained LLM plus massive synthetic TTS data. While this is a legitimate design choice, the paper sometimes frames gains as architectural/full-duplex advances rather than primarily benefits from text pretraining and synthetic supervision.

There is no mathematical proof burden in the paper, but some scientific logic is overstated: outperforming dGSLM in continuation and simulated interaction does not by itself demonstrate human-like full-duplex dialogue or robust internet-scale deployment.
